rows/setup: Multiplying a matrix W by a vector x is written W x, the two side by side, and it is a stack of dot products. Here W has two rows of three, and x has three entries.
rows/row0: Dot the first row of W with x: one times two, plus two times one, plus zero times three. That is four, the first entry of the result.
rows/row1: The second row gives the second entry: six, minus one, plus six. Eleven.
rows/result: So W x is four, eleven: one entry for each row of W.
shapes/match: Each row is dotted with x, so a row and x must be the same length: the number of columns of W must equal the length of x.
shapes/out: And there is one dot product per row, so the result has one entry per row of W. A two by three matrix turns three numbers into two: two by three, times three, gives two, where the at sign is the product and the arrow points to what comes out.
shapes/big: The sizes can be anything. A ten by three thousand and seventy two W turns an image of three thousand and seventy two numbers into ten.
shapes/fail: Give it a vector of the wrong length, and a column of W has no partner: the product is not defined.
paper/flat: In code, a vector is only a list. x has shape three: no rows, no columns. Pages write it across, like this, to save space.
paper/stand: But in W x, x stands as a column, three tall, so each row of W lies across it. Books call that column three by one, and the result two by one.
paper/first: Put a vector first instead, as in v times W, and it lies as a row: v is dotted with each column of W. Two numbers in, three out.
